newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Clock ticks on S.Africa's chance to join trade club.
newsitem.headline: Clock ticks on S.Africa's chance to join trade club.

text.p: The clock is ticking on efforts by South Africa and the European Union to reach an agreement on Pretoria's elevation to a potentially lucrative development club which promises preferential trade and other benefits to members.
Officials from the European Commission -- the EU's executive -- said the two sides ended their latest round of trade talks in Brussels on Wednesday with some advances, but no agreement.
"We made progress on South Africa's partial accession to the Lome treaty and some on bilateral relations," a Commission spokesman said. "But that is all we have done at this point."
Analysts said a short joint statement issued after the meeting was more remarkable for what it left unsaid that what it included.

The statement said work had continued on a draft text setting out the terms and conditions of Pretoria's accession to the Lome Convention -- which governs EU relations with African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) nations -- and also a timetable for bilateral trade talks.
But it noted that the so-called Lome protocol had to be agreed before the next biennial EU-ACP meeting -- in Luxembourg in April -- or the deal could be sidelined for another two years.
The Luxembourg meeting needs to approve the protocol so that South Africa's participation can be ratified by all 70 ACP nations and the 15 EU states.
Partial Lome membership would give South Africa full political representation in the ACP, while excluding it from group development aid.
South Africa already receives over 125 million Ecus ($143 million) a year from the European Union in bilateral aid.
Pretoria would also be eligible for European Development Fund loans and be allowed to tender for lucrative ACP contracts.
The Commission spokesman said South Africa and the EU had also agreed to hold a ministerial meeting later this year to review bilateral trade.

The statement said a provisional timetable was agreed for future talks "on a spectrum of subjects which underline the comprehensive nature of cooperation", but one trade analyst said this could just as easily have read "which underlines the comprehensive nature of differences".

The EU does not want to grant South Africa the substantial trade benefits it offers ACP countries for fear Pretoria's exports would crush those of the bloc -- many of them former colonies of EU nations.
Instead, the EU wants a free-trade deal with South Africa that would exclude certain agricultural products but open a vast new market for European exports.

South Africa, however, has been holding out for a better deal that would include more tariff-free access to European markets for its agricultural exports and also has reservations over what a free-trade deal would mean for its regional partners.

South Africa and the EU have been at odds over what kind of a trade deal to establish since Pretoria emerged from years of apartheid isolation and have been haggling over terms for more than two years.

As well as bilateral trade, the EU is keen to finalise agreements with Pretoria on issues ranging from fisheries to whether imports of South African "sherry" can carry that name or whether that would contravene EU geographical origin laws.
